Ellis Island. A small island in Upper New York Harbor, just off the New Jersey shore near the Statue of Liberty, that served as the primary immigration reception station for the United States from eighteen ninety-two to nineteen fifty-four. Processing over twelve million arrivals—roughly forty percent of all Americans living today have an ancestor who entered through Ellis Island—it became the symbolic gateway to American opportunity and the physical threshold of naturalization. Its geography, situated at the harbor's eastern edge and owned by the federal government, made it the ideal location for immigration bureaucracy.

Located in Upper New York Harbor approximately thirteen hundred feet from the New Jersey coast, yet under federal rather than state jurisdiction, Ellis Island was the venue for centralized immigration processing. The original Oyster Island, its historical name, was expanded through landfill in the eighteen nineties to accommodate the massive immigration station built to replace the crowded Battery Park immigration depot in Manhattan.

Peak arrival years saw five thousand to ten thousand immigrants processed daily. The island handled the wave of Southern and Eastern European migration from eighteen ninety to nineteen twenty that transformed American demographics. New arrivals underwent health inspections including examinations for idiocy, tuberculosis, and other conditions and background checks. Those deemed unfit were deported on return ships.

Symbolically linked to the Statue of Liberty, visible on the island's west side, Ellis Island and the Statue created a composite icon of American immigration and freedom for arriving populations. Officially closed in nineteen fifty-four, the island later abandoned and deteriorated until restoration efforts in the nineteen eighties and nineties converted it into a museum of immigration history.

Ellis Island connects to New York City as the metropolitan hub that received its populations, to the Statue of Liberty as the symbolic neighbor and icon of American welcome and aspiration, to the United States as the nation whose immigration policy Ellis Island administered, to the Atlantic Ocean as the crossing vessel and the oceanic context of transatlantic migration, to New York Harbor as the geographical setting and maritime commerce hub, to immigration as the historical process Ellis Island institutionalized and symbolized, and to New Jersey as the adjacent state with territorial claims disputed in Supreme Court cases.
